summary: Describes a model for setting up IP addresses and subnet prefixes on the interfaces of routers that connect to links whose connectivity is not well defined, as in ad hoc wireless networks. It is informational and not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: In an ad hoc network, routers move around and the link between them may not always work. This memo says how to give those routers addresses and subnet prefixes so that routing still functions: no promises about who is directly reachable, but each address must be unique where the routing protocol needs it.

subtitle: How to configure router interface addresses and subnet prefixes when you cannot know who is on the other end of the link.

tldr.problem: On a link whose connectivity is unplanned or changes over time, there is no standard way to choose the IP address and subnet prefix of a router interface, yet routing protocols need both.
tldr.mechanism: The model gives two rules: configure no on-link subnet prefix on such an interface (for IPv4, any prefix configured must be 32 bits long), and give the interface an address that is unique at least within the routing domain.
tldr.outcome: This is guidance in an Informational document, not a standard. It lets routing protocols and packet forwarding work without promising one-hop reachability to neighbours that may not be there.

today: RFC 5889 is an Informational document from September 2010, not an Internet Standard, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes it and none that updates it. Its two rules are written as guidance for implementers rather than as a protocol to be implemented.

sections.title: The Problem with Links of Undetermined Connectivity
sections.content:
Choosing the right IP addresses and subnet masks for the interfaces of a router is normally a precondition for routing protocols to work. Network designers consider link capabilities, connectivity, geography, available address blocks and expected traffic when they pick a topology and the matching interface configuration.

When the capabilities and connectivity of the links that join routers are well known and stable, that job is straightforward. Without any assumption about link-level connectivity, however, there is no canonical method for deciding what a given interface configuration should be.

Link-level connectivity counts as undetermined when it is unplanned, or when it changes over time. Ad hoc networks are the typical example. Routing protocols for ad hoc networks are deliberately built to detect and maintain paths across the network even across links with undetermined connectivity, on the assumption that the routers' interfaces are configured with IP addresses. This document proposes a model for that configuration, so that routing protocols and data packet forwarding can function.

The scope is deliberately narrow. Routers may need more IP prefixes for applications running on the router itself, or for assignment to attached hosts and networks. For IPv6 those addresses may be global (RFC 3587), Unique-Local (RFC 4193) or Link-Local (RFC 4291); for IPv4 they may be global or private (RFC 1918). Global scope is generally preferred over local scope, though automatic configuration may not always achieve it. The document treats that as a separate problem and concentrates on the addresses and prefixes that routing protocols and forwarding need.
sections.plainLanguage: On a normal network, an engineer can work out in advance which router sits where and give each interface a sensible address. On an ad hoc network the link may work one minute and not the next, so no fixed plan exists. This memo fills that gap with two rules that hold up when the topology is unknown.

sections.title: The Subnet Prefix Principle
sections.content:
If the link an interface connects to gives no basis for assuming connectivity to other interfaces, the only addresses that can be assumed to be on link are the addresses of that interface itself. Link-local addresses are assumed to be on link, but the utility of link-local addresses is limited, as described later in the document.

Subnet prefix configuration on such an interface must therefore make no promise of direct, one-hop IP connectivity to addresses other than the interface's own. That gives the first principle: no on-link subnet prefix should be configured on such an interface.

This is a statement about IP reachability only. If layer 2 communication is enabled between a pair of interfaces, IP packet exchange is also enabled between them, even if the IP subnet configuration is absent or different on each side.

The principle works in one direction only. When assumptions can be made about connectivity between interfaces, or about the persistent reachability of some addresses, those assumptions should be taken into account when configuring subnet prefixes, and the matching interfaces may then be given an on-link subnet prefix. The applicability statement makes the same point: the more specific the assumptions available, the more the configuration should reflect them.
sections.plainLanguage: An on-link subnet prefix tells the router that a whole range of addresses is one hop away. On a link that might not be there tomorrow, that promise cannot be kept, so no on-link prefix is configured. The addresses can still travel over the link, because that depends on the link layer, not on the prefix.

sections.title: The Address Uniqueness Principle
sections.content:
Routing protocols differ in how unique the interface addresses they run on must be. Some impose no uniqueness requirement at all. Others require local uniqueness only, or uniqueness within at least the routing domain, the area of the network under one administrative routing authority (RFC 1136).

Protocols that need no unique IP address within the routing domain carry a separate identifier of their own, which could come from the factory or from configuration. Such a protocol does not care what the IP address is.

Configuring an address that is unique within the routing domain satisfies the less strict requirements as well, and it also supports the protocols with the strictest requirements. That gives the second principle: an IP address assigned to an interface that connects to a link with undetermined connectivity properties should be unique, at least within the routing domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Some routing protocols need the interface address to be unique across the whole routing area, others do not care. Giving every interface an address that is unique in that area satisfies all of them at once, so that is what the model asks for.

sections.title: The IPv6 and IPv4 Models
sections.content:
The two principles give slightly different guidelines for IPv6 and IPv4, because IPv6 offers something IPv4 does not: an interface can simply be left with no on-link subnet prefix at all. The document calls that a cleaner model.

For IPv6 the rules are that the address on the interface should be unique at least within the routing domain, and that no on-link subnet prefix is configured on the interface. An IPv6 link-local address is assigned to each interface anyway (RFC 4291), but in general link-local addresses are of limited utility on links with undetermined connectivity, because connectivity to neighbours may be constantly changing. Two limitations are named. There is in general no mechanism to ensure that IPv6 link-local addresses are unique across multiple links, although link-local addresses that use an interface identifier of the modified EUI-64 form should be globally unique. And routers cannot forward packets with link-local source or destination addresses to other links, while most of the time routers need to forward packets to and from different links. Autoconfiguration solutions should therefore focus on configuring IP addresses that are not IPv6 link-local.

For IPv4 the rules are similar: the address on the interface should be unique at least within the routing domain, and any subnet prefix configured on the interface should be 32 bits long. A prefix of 32 bits names one address, so it makes no claim about any other address being on link. The use of IPv4 link-local addresses (RFC 3927) should be discouraged for most applications, because the limitations above apply to them too. The IPv4 case is worse: the pool of link-local addresses to choose from is smaller, so there is more reliance on Duplicate Address Detection.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 and IPv4 get slightly different rules, but both end up making no promise about neighbours. IPv6 simply has no on-link prefix at all. IPv4 has to use a prefix of 32 bits, which names one address and nothing else. Link-local addresses are discouraged in both cases, because a router cannot forward packets that carry them to another link.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document covers only the address and subnet mask configuration that routing protocols and data packet forwarding need to function. RFC 4593 describes the generic threats to routing protocols, and their applicability is not altered by the presence of interfaces with undetermined connectivity properties. The addressing model described here therefore introduces no new security threats.

There is a caveat. The possible lack of pre-established infrastructure or authority, which the use of interfaces with undetermined connectivity properties allows, may make some of the attacks described in RFC 4593 easier to carry out. In particular, malevolent misconfiguration may be harder to detect and harder to locate.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules add no new attack of their own. But a network that has no fixed infrastructure and no clear authority is a softer target, and a router set up wrongly on purpose is harder to spot and trace.
